title: RBA: Dr Jim has given us anaemia
full_text:
Board warns economy is sick Domestic dysfunction and “anaemic” productivity are the likely drivers of Australia’s rolling inflation nightmare and rising interest rates, the Reserve Bank has warned in a fresh knock to Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ economic record.
Dr Chalmers has consistently blamed rising energy costs from the Iran War for the country’s elevated price pressures, with core inflation now running at 3.6 per cent.
But in the latest minutes from the RBA’s closed-door September meeting, where it hiked the benchmark cash rate to 4.6 per cent, board members said the “upward surprise” in underlying inflation was “more likely” the result of greater domestic capacity pressures than pass-through costs from higher oil prices.
It’s a fresh dig at Dr Chalmers whose spending splurge has jumped 32 per cent since the Albanese government came into power in 2022 and puts a November rate hike – the fifth this year – firmly on the table.
“The RBA has been talking about capacity pressures in the economy for quite a while and we saw inflation in Australia start to accelerate in the second half of 2025, well before the conflict in the Middle East. We had this inflation problem before oil prices started to spike,” Deloitte partner Stephen Smith said.
“Through their (RBA’s) liaison surveys and other data, the evidence that higher fuel prices are feeding into broader prices across the economy is actually pretty limited at the moment.” Mr Smith said the RBA’s patience was “wearing thin”, with the Board warning it would hike rates again if required.
“They know inflation has been above target for too long,” he said. In unusually stark language, the Reserve Bank also warned productivity was “anaemic”.
The IMF’s latest forecast on global growth shows Australia growing at a wobbly 1.6 per cent in 2027, while inflation remains above the top end of the RBA’s 2-3 per cent target band at 3.1 per cent.
It is the highest in all advanced Asian economies, with the exception of Taiwan, and higher than most advanced European economies, behind only Greece, Iceland, Austria and Andorra The US, by contrast, is expected to grow at 2.3 per cent with inflation at 2.8 per cent.
The Board also pointed to the AI investment boom and uncertainty in the Middle East as additional “upside risks” to inflation.
“It’s a bit of everything all at once,” NAB chief economist Dr Sally Auld said, highlighting rising prices for energy, AI-related products and agricultural commodities.
“That’s a bit of a perfect storm and then on top of that you’ve got the domestic story where it is really clear from their liaison survey they (RBA) do and also our NAB business survey that cost pressures are a real issue for many businesses at the moment and they are passing that on to final prices. “At the moment they think the economy can grow at 2 per cent without generating inflation and now they’re like, ‘well we don’t know if that is the right number. It might be a bit less than we think’.”
